explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The man found the treasure, covered it back up, and then went and sold all he had to buy that field (Matthew 13:44). He didn't carry the treasure off in his pockets. He bought the whole field so the treasure came with it. That's a man who read the fine print and loved what he read.

Oxen would be a fine buy if you had a field to plow, friend. But the text says he sold all he had and bought the field where the treasure was (Matthew 13:44). The field was the prize, because the treasure was sitting in it. I'd have bought the dirt too, and I'd have yelled about it.

A vineyard sounds lovely, baker, but it's not in the story. The man sold all he had and bought the field he found the treasure in (Matthew 13:44). Buying the one next door would be like me buying the wrong cooling rack and wondering where my cookies went. He went straight for the right spot.

I get why you'd think so, baker. Selling all you have sounds like a rough Tuesday. But the text says that in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field (Matthew 13:44). Joy is what drives him. So the answer is False. This man is practically skipping to the sale.

That's right, friend. The text says that in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field (Matthew 13:44). No long face and no dragging his feet. I picture a man whose neighbors keep asking why he's smiling at a garage sale of his own stuff.

Yes, baker. When the merchant found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it (Matthew 13:46). He'd been searching for fine pearls, and this one was worth everything he owned. That's a man who knows exactly what he's looking at.

Close, but the text says the opposite, friend. The merchant found one very precious pearl, went away, sold all he had and bought it (Matthew 13:46). He didn't haggle his way out of it or buy it on a payment plan. He gave all he had, and the pearl was his.

That's it, baker. The net was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish (Matthew 13:47). A net doesn't check IDs at the door. Everything swimming through ends up in there together, and the sorting comes later.

Nope, friend, this net isn't picky. The text says it caught all kinds of fish (Matthew 13:47). If it only caught one kind, there'd be nothing to sort later, and the men sit down to sort in the next verse (Matthew 13:48). Think of a big mixed batch, not a single flavor.

That sounds like a good story for the dock, baker. But Jesus says the net caught all kinds of fish (Matthew 13:47). The one very precious item is the pearl in the verse before, so you may have borrowed from it. This net came up full of variety, and no single fish got the spotlight.
Right, baker. They sat down and sorted the good fish into containers, but threw the bad away (Matthew 13:48). The sorting is about good and bad, and nothing else. Nobody's measuring tape comes out.

I can see the logic, friend. Biggest is often best at a bake sale. But the text says the men sorted the good fish into containers and threw the bad away (Matthew 13:48). Size isn't the test here. Good and bad is.

Interesting guess, baker, but the little ones aren't the ones being kept or tossed for being little. The men sorted the good fish into containers and threw the bad away (Matthew 13:48). The line is drawn at good and bad, and size never comes up.

Yes, baker. Jesus says the angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous (Matthew 13:49). This is the part where the fishing picture explains itself. The sorting on the shore matches what happens at the end of the age.

Good guess if you're thinking about who gets the fancy seats, friend. But Jesus says the angels will separate the wicked from the righteous (Matthew 13:49). Money doesn't make the list. The two groups are wicked and righteous.

I see where you're going, baker, since power is what people like to count. But Jesus says the angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous (Matthew 13:49). Being powerful isn't the line. Wicked and righteous are the two groups.

That's what Jesus says, baker. The angels will separate the wicked from the righteous and throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 13:49-50). I think this is a heavy part, and it's okay to say so. Jesus said it plainly, so we hear it plainly.

The fishing picture makes that a natural guess, friend. But Jesus says the angels will throw the wicked into the fiery furnace (Matthew 13:50). The net story is the picture, and the furnace is where Jesus says they go. I think this is a heavy part, so we'll just read it as He said it.

I can see how you landed there, baker. But Jesus doesn't say a pit. He says the angels will throw the wicked into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 13:50). It's a heavy line, so we read it carefully and move on gently.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "Have you understood all these things?" and they answer, "Yes" (Matthew 13:51). The text gives us their answer and nothing more. I'd say that's a pretty confident group after three parables in a row.

Not quite, friend. After Jesus asks, "Have you understood all these things?" the disciples answer, "Yes" (Matthew 13:51). No long pause and no blank looks written in. So the answer is True, and I'm glad I'm not the one who had to answer on the spot.

explanations.answer: New treasures as well as old
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says a scribe discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old (Matthew 13:52). Both kinds come out of the same storeroom. Nothing gets thrown out, and nothing new gets turned away.

Old things are wonderful, friend, and I know a thing or two about being old and stored away. But Jesus says the homeowner brings out new treasures as well as old (Matthew 13:52). The word "new" is right there in the verse. The storeroom holds both.

Fresh is nice, baker, like a warm batch off the rack. But Jesus says the homeowner brings out new treasures as well as old (Matthew 13:52). The old ones count too. He doesn't shop for only what's new, and he doesn't hand out only what's old.
